goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

# jobq

A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
| `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
| `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |

`test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.

## The log

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.

```
limit 2 10
job build 5 ok
job flaky 3 fail ok
submit 0 build
submit 0 flaky
```

`limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.

## The simulation

The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.

## Modes

- `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
- `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.

A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.

## Known gaps

A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

## Summary

I implemented the retry policy, dead-letter mode, and policy-file support for `jobq`, touching only `src/`:

**`src/parse.js`**
- Factored `limit` parsing into `limitDirective` (unchanged behavior).
- Added `retryDirective` for `retry <max> <base>`: exactly two words, `<max>` positive, `<base>` non-negative, at most once, with the exact messages specified (`expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer`, `retry is declared twice`).
- Added `parsePolicy(lines, policy)`: parses a policy file under the same grammar (trim, skip blank/`#` lines), accepting only `limit`/`retry` and refusing anything else with `unknown directive <word>`.

**`src/queue.js`**
- `run` now accepts `policy.retry` and returns `deadLetters` alongside `attempts`/`end`.
- On a `fail` outcome under a retry policy: re-queues the job (same submission `order`, so tie-breaking by submission order is preserved) with `readyAt = finish + base * 2^(attempt-1)` when `attempt < max`, or appends it to `deadLetters` at the fail instant when `attempt === max`.
- No `policy.retry` still means a `fail` is simply final, exactly as before.

**`src/cli.js`**
- New usage: `usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`; mode is `trace|summary|dead`, with 1 or 2 args.
- If a policy path is given, it's read and parsed with `parsePolicy` *before* the log; unreadable files fail as `cannot read policy <path>`, and grammar failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: <message>`. Because the same shared `policy` object is passed into `parse()` for the log, a log line for an already-set directive fails at the log's own line with the normal `... is declared twice` message.
- `summary` now reports `dead` in place of the last-attempt outcome for any dead-lettered job.
- `dead` mode prints one line per dead-lettered job (`<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`) in write-off order, followed by `total <k>`, with no `end` line (per spec, that final line belongs only to `trace`/`summary`).

Verified: full suite `node --test test/*.test.js` passes (34/34), `node_modules` doesn't exist, and manual edge-case checks (invalid `retry` fields, duplicate `retry`, `max=1` immediate dead-lettering, malformed argument lists) all produce the specified messages and exit code 2.

goal.objective:
`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; only addresses inside the addressable range are named. A literal names none, and so does a formula the grammar does not accept; a formula the grammar accepts names its cells whatever the cell evaluates to, so a misplaced range still names every cell it covers.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

- **`src/address.js`** – cell address parsing/formatting (bijective base-26 columns, row ≥ 1 validation, canonical uppercase form, sortable key).

- **`src/values.js`** – literal parsing (numbers/errors/text) and value formatting (10-significant-digit rounding, `TRUE`/`FALSE`, error tokens).

- **`src/deps.js`** – purely syntactic AST walk collecting referenced/range-expanded addresses, independent of which `IF` branch would actually execute.
- **`src/cli.js`** – orchestrates argument validation, stdin reading, sheet parsing, and both `values`/`deps` output modes, buffering all output until the run fully succeeds (nothing written to stdout on failure).

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; only addresses inside the addressable range are named. A literal names none, and so does a formula the grammar does not accept; a formula the grammar accepts names its cells whatever the cell evaluates to, so a misplaced range still names every cell it covers.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

A line is then read as one of these, in this order. 19: 20: A line of three or more backticks with no further backtick on it opens a fenced code block, and its info string is the rest of the line, trimmed, of which the first word is used. The fence closes at the first later line that is nothing but backticks, at least as many as the opening had, and everything between the two is content. A fence that never closes fails. A blank line ends whatever block was open. `#` to `######` followed by a space is a heading of that level, over the trimmed rest of the line. `- ` at the very start of a line is a bullet item, unless a paragraph is already open, in which case it is one of that paragraph's lines. Anything else is a paragraph line, trimmed. 21: 22: Each block renders to `

  • ` per item on its own line, or `
    ` with the content copied in, `class="language-"` when there is an info string. The blocks are joined with newlines and the output ends with one; an empty document renders nothing at all.
23: 
24: ## Inline
25: 
26: A backslash before one of `` \ ` * [ ] ( ) `` writes that character literally. A backtick pair is a code span, with its content escaped. `**` pairs make `` and `*` pairs make ``, each rendering its content inline. `[text](url)` is a link, with the text rendered inline and the url escaped for the attribute. An unmatched marker is literal text. Everything else is escaped for HTML.
27: 
28: ## Modes
29: 
30: - `html` writes the rendered document.
31: - `outline` writes one line per heading, ` `.
32: 
33: ## Failures
34: 
35: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. An unterminated fence is `error: line N: unterminated code fence`, naming the line the fence opened on. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.

39: A list is flat: an indented `- ` is a paragraph line, not a nested item. There are no reference links, so `[text][label]` is literal text and a `[label]: url` line renders as a paragraph. An unmatched marker is literal text. Everything else is escaped for HTML.

Two reference forms are tried after `[text](url)` fails. `[text][label]` uses the written label and `[text][]` uses the link text as the label; the label is normalized the same way a definition's is, and a resolved reference renders as `<a href="<url>">` with the text rendered inline and the url escaped for the attribute. A reference whose label no definition resolves is not a link: the `[` is literal text and scanning continues after it, exactly as an unmatched marker does.

## Modes

- `html` writes the rendered document.
- `outline` writes one line per heading, `<level> <raw heading text>`.
- `defs` writes one line per definition in force, in ascending normalized-label order, `<label> <url> <source>`, where the source is `file` or `document`, followed by a final line `total <k>` counting them.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a definitions file. That file is one definition per line, with a trimmed empty line or one starting with `#` ignored; anything else fails with `error: <file>: line N: expected [label]: <url>`, and a label it defines twice fails with `error: <file>: line N: label <label> is defined twice`, N counting that file's own lines from 1. The file is read before the document, so its failures come first and the document may not redefine what it defined.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js merge|merge2|regions` when the argument is not exactly one of the three mode words, and `error: expected three parts separated by %%%` when the input does not hold exactly three documents. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js merge|merge2|regions` when the argument is not exactly one of the three mode words, and `error: expected three parts separated by %%%` when the input does not hold exactly three documents. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

content.text:
# taskrun

A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
| `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
| `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |

`test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.

## The task file

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.

```
# build.tasks
task build node build.js
task bundle node bundle.js
needs bundle build
```

`task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.

## Modes

- `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
- `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
- `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.

## Known gaps

`order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

## Summary

I extended `taskrun` in `src/` only, adding:

1. **`src/parse.js`** — new `reads <name> <path>...` and `writes <name> <path>...` directives, parsed like `needs` (may precede their `task` line, dedup paths, unknown-name check deferred with existing line-less error). Added path validation (`A-Za-z0-9_./-`, no leading `/`, no `..` segment) producing `error: line N: invalid path <path>`, and the `expected reads/writes <name> <path>...` arity error. Tasks now carry `reads`/`writes` arrays alongside `needs`.

2. **`src/graph.js`** — added a `CycleError` and a `findCycle` depth-first search that visits tasks and their dependencies in ascending name order, returning the first back-edge cycle (from the re-entered task through the stack back to itself). `order()` now throws `CycleError` before computing the topological order, so the existing Kahn's-algorithm loop always completes when it runs (no more silent truncation).

3. **`src/snapshot.js`** (new) — parses a digest snapshot into a `Map<path, digest>`, enforcing the two-word format, the eight-lowercase-hex-digit digest, and duplicate-path detection, each as a `SnapshotError` carrying its own 1-based line number.

4. **`src/cli.js`** — updated usage string; added `files <name>` (prints sorted `reads:`/`writes:` fields, reusing the `-`-for-empty formatter); added `plan <snapshot>` which reads the task file, then the snapshot (`cannot read snapshot <path>` / line-numbered `SnapshotError`s), then walks the graph (`CycleError` → exit 3) and emits `run <name> <reason>`/`skip <name>` lines followed by `total run=<r> skip=<s>`, using the specified precedence: first path reason (`new`/`missing`/`changed`) beats a dependency reason (`needs <dep>`, smallest running dependency).

Verified: full suite (`test/spec.test.js` + `test/taskrun.test.js`, 35 tests) passes; no `node_modules` exists; manually probed additional corner cases not covered by the visible suite (absolute paths, `..` mid-segment vs. as a segment, directives before their task, unknown names, usage arity for every mode, multi-node cycles found deeper in the DFS, empty/short-digest snapshots) and all matched the specification's wording and exit codes.
