1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

</content>

1: /** The INI reader: dotted keys and the raw text of each value. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an INI line, carrying the 1-based line and column it was read at. */
6: export class IniError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, column, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'IniError'
15:     this.line = line
16:     this.column = column
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
21: function indent(raw) {
22:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
23: }
24: 
25: /**
26:  * Parse INI text into its settings.
27:  * @param {string} text - the file's whole text.
28:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} each dotted key's raw value, in the order the file writes them.
29:  * @throws {IniError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
30:  */
31: export function parse(text) {
32:   const lines = text.split('\n')
33:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
34:   const values = new Map()
35:   let section = ''
36:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
37:     const line = index + 1
38:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
39:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#') || trimmed.startsWith(';')) continue
40:     if (trimmed.startsWith('[')) {
41:       if (!trimmed.endsWith(']')) throw new IniError(line, raw.trimEnd().length + 1, 'expected "]"')
42:       const name = trimmed.slice(1, -1)
43:       if (name === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, 'expected a section name')
44:       if (!NAME.test(name)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, `invalid section name ${name}`)
45:       section = name
46:       continue
47:     }
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a section header or key = value')
50:     const key = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (key === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + split, 'expected a key')
52:     if (!NAME.test(key)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `invalid key ${key}`)
53:     const full = section === '' ? key : `${section}.${key}`
54:     if (values.has(full)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `key ${full} is set twice`)
55:     values.set(full, trimmed.slice(split + 1).trim())
56:   }
57:   return values
58: }

1: /** Stacking layers: the last layer that sets a key wins. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * Merge named layers, later over earlier.
5:  * @param {readonly {name: string, values: Map<string, string>}[]} layers - the layers, weakest first.
6:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} each key's winning raw text.
7:  */
8: export function merge(layers) {
9:   const merged = new Map()
10:   for (const layer of layers) {
11:     for (const [key, text] of layer.values) merged.set(key, text)
12:   }
13:   return merged
14: }

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `dump <file>` and `get <file> <key>`. */
3: 
4: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { IniError, parse as parseIni } from './ini.js'
6: import { merge } from './layer.js'
7: import { SETTINGS, setting } from './schema.js'
8: 
9: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>'
10: 
11: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
12: function fail(message) {
13:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
14:   process.exit(2)
15: }
16: 
17: /** One INI layer, refused at its own position when the grammar rejects it. */
18: function iniLayer(name, path) {
19:   if (!existsSync(path)) fail(`cannot read ${path}`)
20:   try {
21:     return { name, values: parseIni(readFileSync(path, 'utf8')) }
22:   } catch (error) {
23:     if (!(error instanceof IniError)) throw error
24:     return fail(`${path}:${error.line}:${error.column}: ${error.message}`)
25:   }
26: }
27: 
28: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
29: const mode = argv[0]
30: const arity = { dump: 2, get: 3 }
31: if (argv.length !== arity[mode]) fail(USAGE)
32: 
33: const values = merge([iniLayer('file', argv[1])])
34: const raw = key => (values.has(key) ? values.get(key) : setting(key).default)
35: const out = []
36: if (mode === 'dump') {
37:   for (const declared of SETTINGS) out.push(`${declared.key}=${raw(declared.key)}`)
38: } else {
39:   if (setting(argv[2]) === undefined) fail(`unknown setting ${argv[2]}`)
40:   out.push(raw(argv[2]))
41: }
42: process.stdout.write(out.map(line => `${line}\n`).join(''))

13:   { key: 'server.tls', type: 'boolean', default: 'false' },
14:   { key: 'tags', type: 'list', default: '' },
15: ]
16: 
17: const BY_KEY = new Map(SETTINGS.map(declared => [declared.key, declared]))
18: 
19: /**
20:  * The setting one key names, or undefined when the schema does not know it.
21:  * @param {string} key - the dotted setting key.
22:  * @returns {{key: string, type: string, members?: string[], default: string} | undefined} the setting.
23:  */
24: export function setting(key) {

1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

(End of file - total 55 lines)
</content>

A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
| `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
| `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |

`test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.

## The INI grammar

A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.

```ini
log.file = /var/log/app.log

[server]
port = 9090
```

## The schema

| Key | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `log.file` | string | (empty) |
| `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
| `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
| `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
| `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
| `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
| `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
| `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
| `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
| `tags` | list | (empty) |

The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.

## Modes

- `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
- `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.

## Known gaps

Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. `load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

1: # taskrun
2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

2: 
3: const OFFSET = 0x811c9dc5
4: const PRIME = 16777619
5: 
6: /**
7:  * The 32-bit FNV-1a digest of a byte buffer as eight lowercase hex digits.
8:  * @param {Buffer} bytes - the bytes to digest.
9:  * @returns {string} the digest.
10:  */
11: export function digestBytes(bytes) {
12:   let hash = OFFSET >>> 0
13:   for (const byte of bytes) {
14:     hash = (hash ^ byte) >>> 0
15:     hash = Math.imul(hash, PRIME) >>> 0
16:   }

{
  "id": "code:task-runner",
  "tier": 6,
  "domain": "systems",
  "title": "Teach taskrun file dependencies, cycle detection, and an incremental plan",
  "prompt": "`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.\n\nTwo directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.\n\n`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.\n\n`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.\n\n`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.\n\nA task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.",

---README---
# taskrun

A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
| `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
| `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |

`test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.

## The task file

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.

```
# build.tasks
task build node build.js
task bundle node bundle.js
needs bundle build
```

`task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.

## Modes

- `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
- `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
- `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.

## Known gaps

`order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js replay|summary` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unknown directive <word>`, `expected bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>`, `expected window <name> <limit> <span>`, `expected route <prefix> <policy>...`, `expected event <tick> <key>`, `invalid policy name <name>`, `invalid route prefix <prefix>`, `invalid key <key>`, `policy <name> is declared twice`, `prefix <prefix> is routed twice`, `unknown policy <name>`, `declarations must come before the first event`, `tick T is before tick P`, and `<field> must be an integer of at least <least>` naming the field as `capacity`, `refill`, `per`, `limit`, `span` or `tick`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

{
  "id": "code:rate-limit-sim",
  "tier": 5,
  "domain": "systems",
  "title": "Replay an event log through token buckets and sliding windows",
  "prompt": "`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.\n\nA name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.\n\n`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.\n\nEach policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.\n\nA token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.\n\nA sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.\n\n`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.\n\nA failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js replay|summary` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unknown directive <word>`, `expected bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>`, `expected window <name> <limit> <span>`, `expected route <prefix> <policy>...`, `expected event <tick> <key>`, `invalid policy name <name>`, `invalid route prefix <prefix>`, `invalid key <key>`, `policy <name> is declared twice`, `prefix <prefix> is routed twice`, `unknown policy <name>`, `declarations must come before the first event`, `tick T is before tick P`, and `<field> must be an integer of at least <least>` naming the field as `capacity`, `refill`, `per`, `limit`, `span` or `tick`.",

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js replay|summary` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unknown directive <word>`, `expected bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>`, `expected window <name> <limit> <span>`, `expected route <prefix> <policy>...`, `expected event <tick> <key>`, `invalid policy name <name>`, `invalid route prefix <prefix>`, `invalid key <key>`, `policy <name> is declared twice`, `prefix <prefix> is routed twice`, `unknown policy <name>`, `declarations must come before the first event`, `tick T is before tick P`, and `<field> must be an integer of at least <least>` naming the field as `capacity`, `refill`, `per`, `limit`, `span` or `tick`. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.
